item.text:
<thoughtml version="1.0">
  <context>
    <scenario>School tutoring trial evaluation</scenario>
    <question>What do the results suggest, what are the key limitations, what causal story is most plausible, and how confident should the school be about adoption?</question>
  </context>

  <findings>
    <finding id="f1" strength="moderate">
      <claim>Students who participated in tutoring improved more than the comparison class.</claim>
      <interpretation>This is consistent with a positive program effect.</interpretation>
    </finding>
    <finding id="f2" strength="moderate">
      <claim>Teachers observed better homework completion among tutoring participants.</claim>
      <interpretation>Homework completion may be one mechanism through which tutoring helps academic performance.</interpretation>
    </finding>
    <finding id="f3" strength="weak">
      <claim>Attendance gains were small.</claim>
      <interpretation>Attendance does not appear to be a major driver of the observed improvement.</interpretation>
    </finding>
  </findings>

  <limitations>
    <limitation id="l1" severity="high" type="selection_bias">
      <claim>Participation was voluntary.</claim>
      <impact>Students who chose tutoring may differ systematically from nonparticipants.</impact>
    </limitation>
    <limitation id="l2" severity="high" type="confounding">
      <claim>The tutoring group began with more motivated families.</claim>
      <impact>Family motivation could independently increase student improvement and homework completion.</impact>
    </limitation>
    <limitation id="l3" severity="medium" type="causal_inference">
      <claim>The comparison does not establish random assignment.</claim>
      <impact>The observed advantage cannot be interpreted as a clean causal estimate of tutoring alone.</impact>
    </limitation>
    <limitation id="l4" severity="low" type="measurement">
      <claim>Teacher observations may contain subjective judgment.</claim>
      <impact>Homework-related improvements are informative but not fully independent evidence.</impact>
    </limitation>
  </limitations>

  <causal_hypothesis>
    <primary>
      <claim>Tutoring likely contributed to academic improvement by increasing structure, support, and homework completion.</claim>
    </primary>
    <alternative>
      <claim>Part of the observed improvement may reflect preexisting family motivation rather than tutoring itself.</claim>
    </alternative>
    <mechanism_assessment>
      <supported_pathway>Improved homework completion and engagement</supported_pathway>
      <weak_pathway>Attendance change</weak_pathway>
    </mechanism_assessment>
    <net_judgment>The most plausible view is that tutoring helped, but the size of its effect is probably overstated by selection effects.</net_judgment>
  </causal_hypothesis>

  <adoption_confidence level="moderate" stance="guarded_adopt">
    <summary>The program is promising enough to continue or expand cautiously, but the evidence is not strong enough to treat the current result as definitive proof.</summary>
    <reasoning>
      <point>Outcome patterns are directionally positive.</point>
      <point>Observed homework improvements support a plausible mechanism.</point>
      <point>Voluntary participation and higher initial family motivation substantially reduce causal certainty.</point>
    </reasoning>
    <recommendation>Adopt provisionally while running a stronger follow-up evaluation with better matching or random assignment if feasible.</recommendation>
  </adoption_confidence>
</thoughtml>
